title: Ending AI Slop — Thais Castello Branco, Taste Labs

primary.label: AI Data Engineering
primary.rationale: The talk's central focus is building high-signal preference data, expert labeling, data quality methodology, decomposition for data grading, and curation for subjective domains. Preference data is an explicit example topic in this category. The speaker details controllable data quality factors (expert selection, problem decomposition, QA checks), preference vector construction, and quality-over-quantity data strategy—all core data engineering concerns for AI systems.

secondary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
secondary.rationale: The talk discusses RL environments for taste, post-training data pipelines, and how preference data feeds into model training. Decomposed components are routed to RL environments or post-training data depending on verifiability. The framing of capability following measurability directly relates to post-training adaptation in subjective domains.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: Taste Labs works with frontier labs on benchmarking and evaluation. Decomposition creates element-level grading criteria that function as evaluation rubrics. The talk compares human judgment versus LLM-as-a-judge for subjective domains, addressing evaluation methodology and judge reliability.

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: The primary application domain is creative production: design, brand adherence, creative writing, and visual aesthetics. The Reduct brand example and the community of over a thousand expert designers directly map to media and creative systems.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The methodology of decomposition, preference vectors, and data quality is presented as cross-domain, applicable to any subjective domain including emotional intelligence and personality, not limited to creative media.

summary: Thais Castello Branco, founder and CEO of Taste Labs, presents the company's mission to end "AI slop" by building data and infrastructure for subjective domains—design, creative writing, emotional intelligence—where AI models still lag behind objective domains like coding and math. She identifies two root causes: (1) capability follows measurability, meaning models improve when tasks can be decomposed, verified, and executed cleanly, and (2) collapse to the mean, where models predict the most likely output, which in creative domains is neither optimal nor great, producing the repetitive, average feeling of AI slop. Her core methodology is decomposition: breaking fuzzy tasks like brand adherence into codifiable, gradable elements (colors, typography, motion, textures) that can serve as ground truth for RL environments or human judgment. She introduces a verifiable-to-preference spectrum and a routing framework that assigns each decomposed component to the best solution method—RL environments, post-training data, context/inference-time, or human judgment. She argues human judgment still exceeds LLM-as-a-judge for subjective domains due to reward hacking and hallucination in automated judges. She then addresses preference data collapse: collecting preferences without understanding who reviewers are and why they like what they like produces noisy data that collapses again to the mean. Her solution is a preference vector per individual, enabling intentional pluralism rather than averaging contradictory tastes. For data quality, she identifies controllable factors: strict expert selection, problem decomposition, and QA checks that look for high-signal properties like specificity of expert language and tying commentary to specific code components. Human QA must distinguish disagreement on objective elements like alignment (a data flaw) from disagreement on style or aesthetics (valuable preference-diversity signal). She closes advocating quality over quantity: expensive, high-signal data from high-taste experts with proper decomposition far outperforms large volumes of noisy data. Taste Labs works with frontier labs on benchmarking and with agent companies on context and user intent; the talk focuses on model training while a companion talk covers agent-side work.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly coupled pipeline for improving AI performance in subjective domains. The AI concepts (collapse to the mean, capability follows measurability, preference data collapse, LLM-as-a-judge limitations) diagnose why current models produce AI slop—identifying problems at both the model behavior level and the data collection level. The software engineering concepts (decomposition methodology, routing logic, code-component tying, QA workflow design, preference vector schema, RL environment design) provide the engineering toolkit to address those diagnoses. Decomposition is the bridge: it converts the AI-level insight that "capability follows measurability" into a concrete practice of breaking fuzzy tasks into graded elements. Routing logic then operationalizes the verifiable-to-preference spectrum, deciding which elements go to automated training (RL environments) versus human judgment. Preference vectors solve the data-side collapse problem that mirrors the model-side mode collapse problem. QA workflows ensure that the human annotation pipeline produces high-signal data without suppressing legitimate preference diversity. Together, these concepts describe an end-to-end system: diagnose the slop problem (AI concepts), decompose subjective tasks into measurable elements (decomposition), route each element to the right training method (routing), collect high-signal preference data with identity-aware aggregation (preference vectors), and QA the entire pipeline to separate objective flaws from subjective diversity (QA workflows). Without the AI concepts, the engineering practices lack motivation; without the engineering practices, the AI diagnoses lack a remedy.
temporalContext: This video was published on July 31, 2026, approximately six weeks after Taste Labs emerged from stealth on June 16, 2026. The talk represents an early public elaboration of the company's methodology and framework, coinciding with the broader industry conversation about AI-generated content quality ("AI slop") that intensified throughout 2025-2026 as generative models became widely deployed for creative tasks. At this time, RLHF and preference data collection were well-established practices, but their limitations in subjective domains were becoming increasingly apparent. The talk reflects the emerging industry recognition that data quality and decomposition—not just model scaling—are critical bottlenecks for creative AI applications. Taste Labs was actively hiring (8+ open roles as of August 2026) and had secured most frontier labs as customers, indicating strong market demand for this approach. Research as of August 23, 2026.
takeaways: Capability follows measurability: solving even part of the measurability problem unlocks large gains in subjective domains.
Decomposition is the core move—break fuzzy outputs like brand into elements that can each be graded against ground truth.
Collapse to the mean is the deeper problem: models predict the most likely output, which in creative domains is neither optimal nor great.
Preference data also collapses to the mean when collected without understanding who reviewers are and why they like what they like; preference vectors enable intentional pluralism.
High-signal data correlates with specificity of expert language and tying commentary to specific code or design components rather than vague paragraph descriptions.
Human QA must distinguish disagreement on objective elements like alignment (a data flaw) from disagreement on style or aesthetics (valuable preference-diversity signal).
Quality over quantity: expensive, high-signal data from high-taste experts outperforms large volumes of noisy, unintentional data.
Routing logic determines whether each decomposed component is best solved via RL environments, post-training data, context, or human judgment.
Human judgment still exceeds LLM-as-a-judge for subjective domains due to reward hacking and hallucination in automated judges.

concepts.name: AI slop
concepts.explanation: The phenomenon of AI-generated content feeling repetitive, average, and lacking creativity or taste, caused by models collapsing to the mean and producing the most likely rather than the most optimal or creative output.
concepts.importance: This is the core problem the talk and Taste Labs aim to solve—it frames the entire motivation for building better data and infrastructure for subjective domains.

concepts.name: Capability follows measurability
concepts.explanation: The principle that AI model capability in a domain is gated by the ability to measure and verify outputs—domains like coding and math excel because they are decomposable and verifiable, while subjective domains lag because they resist these properties.
concepts.importance: This is one of two foundational root-cause explanations in the talk, establishing why solving even part of the measurability problem unlocks large gains in subjective domains.

concepts.name: Collapse to the mean (mode collapse)
concepts.explanation: The tendency of generative models to predict the most likely output and treat it as ideal, which works for math but not for creative work where greatness lives at the tails of the distribution. This produces repetitive, average-feeling outputs characteristic of AI slop.
concepts.importance: This is the second foundational root-cause explanation, linking a known model behavior problem to the user-facing experience of AI slop and motivating the need for techniques that force distribution toward creative ends.

concepts.name: LLM-as-a-judge limitations
concepts.explanation: Automated LLM-based evaluation of subjective outputs is unreliable due to reward hacking and hallucination patterns. Human judgment still exceeds LLM-as-a-judge for subjective domains like design and brand adherence.
concepts.importance: This establishes a critical constraint on automated evaluation pipelines—any solution for subjective domains must account for the fact that automated judges cannot yet replace human experts in these areas.

concepts.name: Preference data collapse
concepts.explanation: When preference data is collected without understanding who reviewers are, what they like, and why, the resulting dataset becomes noisy and collapses to averaged preferences, destroying the pluralistic signal needed for training models that serve diverse tastes.
concepts.importance: This identifies a specific failure mode in RLHF-style data collection that is distinct from mode collapse in the model—it occurs at the data level and must be addressed through preference vectors and identity-aware aggregation.

concepts.name: Preference vectors for pluralism
concepts.explanation: A per-individual vector representation of preferences that enables intentional pluralism in training data, preserving diverse tastes rather than averaging contradictory signals into noise. This is the proposed solution to preference data collapse.
concepts.importance: This is the core AI-level innovation proposed in the talk for the data side of the problem, complementing decomposition on the task side.

concepts.name: Reward hacking in automated evaluation
concepts.explanation: A failure mode where automated judges (LLMs) find ways to score well on evaluation metrics without genuinely satisfying the underlying subjective criteria, making them unreliable for grading design, brand adherence, or creative quality.
concepts.importance: This is a key reason why human judgment remains necessary for subjective domains and why routing logic must account for verifiability when deciding between automated and human evaluation.

concepts.name: Verifiable-to-preference spectrum
concepts.explanation: A conceptual spectrum along which elements of a subjective task are classified, ranging from programmatically verifiable components (suitable for RL environments) to pure preference and creativity components (requiring human judgment). The most valuable work lies in between.
concepts.importance: This spectrum is the analytical framework that drives routing decisions and determines which training or evaluation method is appropriate for each decomposed component.

concepts.name: Quality over quantity in training data
concepts.explanation: The principle that expensive, high-signal data from high-taste experts with proper problem decomposition yields far better model results than large volumes of noisy, unintentional data. Controllable quality factors include expert selection, specificity, and commentary-to-component tying.
concepts.importance: This is the closing strategic recommendation of the talk, with direct implications for data budgeting and pipeline design in AI organizations working on subjective domains.

concepts.name: Post-training data pipelines for subjective domains
concepts.explanation: Data pipelines that route decomposed subjective task components to appropriate post-training methods, including RL environments for verifiable elements and curated human preference data for contextual or preference-dependent elements.
concepts.importance: This connects the decomposition and routing methodology to actual post-training workflows used by frontier labs, showing how the framework integrates into existing training infrastructure.

concepts.name: Decomposition methodology for subjective tasks
concepts.explanation: Breaking fuzzy, hard-to-measure tasks like brand adherence into individual codifiable elements (colors, typography, motion, textures) that can each be graded against ground truth, turning subjective judgment into a tractable engineering problem.
concepts.importance: This is the central engineering practice of the talk—it transforms unmeasurable creative tasks into measurable, verifiable sub-problems that can feed into RL environments or human judgment pipelines.

concepts.name: Routing logic for solution method selection
concepts.explanation: A framework that takes decomposed task elements and assigns each to the most appropriate solution method—RL environments, post-training data, context/inference-time, or human judgment—based on where each element falls on the verifiable-to-preference spectrum.
concepts.importance: Routing is the key architectural decision that determines how each component of a subjective task is processed, enabling a hybrid pipeline that leverages both automated and human judgment optimally.

concepts.name: Code-component tying for training data quality
concepts.explanation: A data engineering practice where expert commentary on a design or code output is explicitly linked to specific code components rather than given as vague paragraph descriptions, producing less noisy and higher-signal training data.
concepts.importance: This is a concrete, implementable technique for improving the signal-to-noise ratio of expert annotation data, directly impacting model training quality in subjective domains.

concepts.name: Human QA workflow design for subjective data
concepts.explanation: A QA process that distinguishes expert disagreement on objective elements like alignment or spacing (flagged as data flaws) from disagreement on subjective elements like style or aesthetics (treated as valuable preference-diversity signal), ensuring data quality without suppressing legitimate taste variation.
concepts.importance: This workflow is essential for maintaining data integrity in subjective domains where disagreement is not always error—misclassifying legitimate preference diversity as flaws would destroy the pluralistic signal that the methodology aims to preserve.

concepts.name: RL environment design for subjective domains
concepts.explanation: Constructing reinforcement learning environments where AI-generated outputs (e.g., a brand-adherent web page) are graded against decomposed ground-truth criteria rather than mere replication of an original, enabling automated training on subjective quality.
concepts.importance: This bridges the gap between subjective human judgment and automated training pipelines, making it possible to scale RL-based improvement in domains that previously resisted programmatic evaluation.

concepts.name: Preference vector schema for pluralistic data aggregation
concepts.explanation: A data structure that captures each individual reviewer's preferences as a vector, enabling aggregation that preserves pluralism rather than averaging contradictory tastes into noise. This replaces naive preference averaging with intentional, identity-aware data combination.
concepts.importance: This is the engineering mechanism for avoiding preference data collapse, ensuring that the training pipeline receives differentiated signal rather than homogenized averages.

sections.title: Introduction and Taste Labs Mission
sections.summary: Thais introduces Taste Labs, recently out of stealth, with a mission to end AI slop by decomposing and understanding subjective domains where AI still lags behind objective ones like coding and math.

sections.title: Two Modes of Working with Labs and Agent Companies
sections.summary: Taste Labs works with frontier labs on evaluation, benchmarking, and determining whether problems need RL environments or post-training data, and with agent/application companies on context and user intent for a world of billions of non-expert creators.

sections.title: Why Subjective Domains Are Harder
sections.summary: Most of the world is subjective with no single right answer. Code is verifiable because of properties of code itself, not models. Two fundamental challenges are identified: capability follows measurability, and collapse to the mean.

sections.title: Decomposing Design and the Brand Example
sections.summary: Great design is contextual and time-varying. Using the Reduct brand as an example, she shows how decomposing a brand into colors, typography, motion, textures creates codifiable elements that can serve as ground truth for RL environments, turning fuzzy judgment into a verifiable task.

sections.title: The Verifiable-to-Preference Spectrum and Routing
sections.summary: Design contains elements ranging from objective to hard-to-measure. The routing problem is breaking a fuzzy task into components and selecting the best solution method for each.

sections.title: Collapse to the Mean
sections.summary: Models predict the most likely outcome and treat it as ideal, which works for math but not for creative work where greatness lives at the ends of the distribution. This mode collapse and repetition produces the feeling of being surrounded by AI slop.

sections.title: Pulling Fuzzy Problems Toward Verification
sections.summary: She introduces pulling subjective tasks toward verification through codification. Brand adherence is hard for humans to judge holistically but becomes tractable when codified into observable, measurable elements. Human taste still exceeds LLM-as-a-judge.

sections.title: Preference Vectors and Avoiding Preference Data Collapse
sections.summary: Preference data collected without understanding who reviewers are and why they like what they like collapses again to the mean. The solution is a preference vector per individual, enabling intentional pluralism of preferences instead of averaging contradictory signals into noise.

sections.title: Data Quality: Controllable Factors and Human QA
sections.summary: Data quality in subjective domains depends on controllable factors: strict expert selection, problem decomposition, and QA checks for high-signal properties like specificity of language and tying commentary to specific code components. Human QA must distinguish disagreement on objective elements (a flaw) from disagreement on style or aesthetics (valuable preference-diversity signal). Because labs often don't provide feedback loops on what data drove which improvement, focusing on controllable quality factors is essential.

sections.title: Quality Over Quantity
sections.summary: She closes advocating a quality-over-quantity approach for subjective domain data: expensive, high-signal data produced by high-taste experts with proper problem decomposition yields far better model results than large volumes of noisy, unintentional data.

demonstrations: Decomposing the Reduct brand into colors, typography, motion, animation, and textures as a worked example of turning fuzzy design judgment into codifiable, verifiable elements.
Designing a task where an agent creates a new brand-adherent page graded against decomposed ground truth rather than mere replication of the original.
Tying expert commentary on a landing page to specific code components to produce less noisy, higher-signal training data.
limitations: LLM-as-a-judge is unreliable for subjective domains due to reward hacking and hallucination patterns.
Brand adherence judged holistically by an LLM is quite hard; only decomposed element-by-element grading makes it tractable.
Subjective quality standards change over time, unlike math or code, complicating static benchmarks.
The average (most likely) output is not the optimal output in creative domains, undermining standard model training objectives.
Collecting preference data without understanding reviewer identity and reasoning collapses back to noisy averages.
When working with labs, the feedback loop on exactly what data caused which model improvement is often unavailable.
quantitativeClaims: Taste Labs works with a community of over a thousand expert designers across different media and styles.
The speaker predicts billions of non-expert people will be creating content, making user-intent understanding as important as model improvement.

organization.name: Taste Labs
organization.summary: Taste Labs is a San Francisco-based AI infrastructure company founded by Thais Castello Branco in October 2025. The company emerged from stealth on June 16, 2026 with $18.5M seed funding co-led by CRV and Amplify Partners. Taste Labs builds data and infrastructure for measuring, codifying, and evaluating subjective domains, starting with design. It operates in two modes: working with frontier AI labs on post-training data, RL environments, and evaluation/benchmarking, and working with app-layer and agent companies on context and verification tools. The company self-describes as a hybrid research lab and infra product company with a team of approximately 18, runs the TasteMakers curated community of over 1,000 expert designers, offers the Taste Engine API for brand/design guideline extraction, and runs a Prototype fellowship for researchers. Active hiring across research, engineering, product, and operations.
organization.status: Active, post-stealth, actively hiring across research, engineering, product, and operations. Shipping products including Taste Engine API and TasteMakers community platform.

technologies.label: Decomposition & Routing for Subjective Domain Training
technologies.summary: The talk's central methodology is decomposition: breaking fuzzy, hard-to-measure tasks like brand adherence into individual codifiable elements (colors, typography, motion, textures) that can each be graded against ground truth. This transforms subjective judgment into a tractable engineering problem. A verifiable-to-preference spectrum classifies each decomposed element, and routing logic assigns each to the most appropriate solution method — RL environments for verifiable components, post-training data for semi-verifiable ones, context/inference-time for contextual elements, and human judgment for pure preference. The Reduct brand example demonstrates decomposing a brand into elements that serve as ground-truth criteria for an RL environment where an agent creates brand-adherent pages graded element-by-element. This approach is motivated by the principle that capability follows measurability and by the need to counteract collapse to the mean, where models predict average outputs that feel like AI slop.
technologies.role: This is the core engineering methodology of the talk, presented as Taste Labs' primary approach to making subjective domains tractable for AI model training. The decomposition framework with the Reduct brand example occupies the largest portion of the talk.

technologies.label: Preference Vector Infrastructure for Pluralistic Data
technologies.primary: Preference vectors for pluralistic data aggregation
technologies.summary: The talk identifies preference data collapse as a distinct failure mode from model-level mode collapse: when preference data is collected without understanding who reviewers are, what they like, and why, the resulting dataset becomes noisy and collapses to averaged preferences, destroying the pluralistic signal needed for training models that serve diverse tastes. The proposed solution is a preference vector per individual — a vector representation of each reviewer's preferences that enables intentional pluralism in training data, preserving diverse tastes rather than averaging contradictory signals into noise. Code-component tying complements this by ensuring expert commentary is anchored to specific code or design components, reducing noise at the collection stage before aggregation.
technologies.role: Presented as the data-side counterpart to the decomposition methodology — while decomposition solves the task-side measurability problem, preference vectors solve the preference-side collapse problem. Together they form the two pillars of Taste Labs' approach.

technologies.label: Human Expert Evaluation & QA for Subjective Domains
technologies.primary: Human QA workflow design for subjective data
technologies.summary: The talk argues that human judgment still exceeds LLM-as-a-judge for subjective domains due to reward hacking and hallucination patterns in automated judges. This necessitates human-in-the-loop evaluation infrastructure. The QA workflow must distinguish expert disagreement on objective elements like alignment or spacing (flagged as data flaws) from disagreement on subjective elements like style or aesthetics (treated as valuable preference-diversity signal). High-signal data correlates with specificity of expert language and tying commentary to specific code or design components. The TasteMakers community of 1,000+ expert designers, recruited through a trust-propagation model, provides the human judgment infrastructure for these workflows.
technologies.role: Establishes the evaluation methodology layer of the talk's framework — after decomposition and routing determine what to evaluate, human QA workflows determine how to evaluate reliably, and why automated judges cannot yet replace human experts in subjective domains.

technologies.label: Taste Labs Data & Infrastructure Platform
technologies.summary: Taste Labs is the featured company and platform embodying the talk's entire methodology. Founded by Thais Castello Branco in October 2025, the company emerged from stealth on June 16, 2026 with $18.5M seed co-led by CRV and Amplify Partners. It operates a two-sided business: working with frontier labs on post-training data, RL environments, and evaluation/benchmarking, and with agent/app-layer companies on context and user-intent tools. The platform integrates decomposition, routing, preference vectors, and human QA workflows into a data infrastructure product. The closing advocacy for quality-over-quantity — expensive high-signal data from high-taste experts outperforming large volumes of noisy data — is both a strategic recommendation and the core value proposition of the Taste Labs platform.
technologies.role: The Taste Labs platform is the subject of the entire talk — the speaker presents the company's mission, methodology, and approach as a unified framework for ending AI slop in subjective domains.
